title: Landscape ecology

definition.text: The science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across a range of landscape scales and spatial patterns.

facts.text: It treats landscapes as spatially uneven areas of interacting patches or ecosystems, from forests, grasslands and lakes to farmland and towns.
Its hallmarks are a focus on how pattern, process and scale relate, and on broad-scale ecological and environmental problems.
Where traditional ecology often assumes spatially uniform systems, landscape ecology builds on heterogeneity in space and time.
The German geographer Carl Troll coined the term Landschaftsökologie in 1939, from aerial-photograph studies of how environment and vegetation interact.
It was an established discipline by 1980, marked by the founding of the International Association for Landscape Ecology in 1982.
It relies on remote sensing, GIS and models; one application estimates soil carbon across a region from landform, vegetation types and rainfall data.
It also draws on geomorphology, the study of how geological formations give a landscape its structure.
It treats humans explicitly as agents that change landscapes, and proposes ways to restore degraded ones.

notes: Soil science lists landscape ecology among its related disciplines (S:90d1e8737433).

title: Spatial heterogeneity
article: Landscape ecology#Scale and heterogeneity (incorporating composition, structure, and function)

definition.text: The uneven distribution of objects across a landscape, a measure of how its parts differ from one another.

facts.text: Heterogeneity is the key element that sets landscape ecology apart from other branches of ecology.
Scale, another main concept, is both the ratio of map to ground distance and the spatial or temporal extent or resolution of an object or process.
Composition is the number and relative abundance of patch types, such as the amount of forest or wetland; structure adds how those patches are arranged and proportioned.
The landscape stability principle holds that structural heterogeneity helps a landscape resist and recover from disturbance.

definition.text: A patch is a relatively uniform area that differs from its surroundings; the mosaic is the whole pattern of patches, corridors and matrix that makes up a landscape.

facts.text: Patches are the basic units of a landscape, and they change and fluctuate in a process called patch dynamics.
The matrix is a landscape's well-connected background system; connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is.
Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides, and a network is a set of linked corridors.
Repeated clearing beyond a critical level breaks continuous cover into isolated patches, so landscapes show a connected and a disconnected phase.

definition.text: A transitional zone between two communities, one kind of boundary between landscape patches.

facts.text: Ecotones may be natural, like a lakeshore, or human-made, like a field cleared from forest; forest-to-marshland transitions and riparian zones are classic examples.
An ecotone keeps traits of both neighbouring communities and often holds species found in neither.
An ecocline, by contrast, is a gradual, continuous change in environmental conditions across an ecosystem or community.
An ecotope is the smallest ecologically distinct unit used to map and classify landscapes.

definition.text: Soil that is permanently or seasonally saturated with water, so that it turns anaerobic, as in wetlands.

facts.text: Most soils are aerobic: roots, most microorganisms and soil animals such as earthworms need oxygen, which moves through connected pores.
When rain or flooding saturates a soil, gas diffusion slows some 10,000 times because no open passages for air remain.
If anaerobic conditions last long in the growing season, biological and chemical reactions different from those of aerobic soils take over.
Saturation that is prolonged and repeated over many years produces distinctive properties recognizable in the field; soils with them are called hydric.
Hydric soils may occupy only a small part of a landscape, yet they keep important soil functions.
Their plants often have aerenchyma, internal air spaces that carry oxygen down to the roots.
Swamps and marshes form along waterbodies with rich hydric soils, and the soils of freshwater marshes are hydric.
A gleysol is a hydric soil saturated by groundwater long enough to develop a characteristic gleyic colour pattern.

definition.text: In US federal law, a soil that, undrained, is saturated, flooded or ponded long enough in the growing season to become anaerobic and support water-loving vegetation.

facts.text: The term is part of the legal definition of a wetland in the Food Security Act of 1985, used by the Natural Resources Conservation Service to administer its 'Swampbuster' provisions.
Congress required waterlogging long enough to support not only the growth but also the regeneration of plants adapted to anaerobic conditions.
The National Technical Committee for Hydric Soils defines it as soil formed under saturation, flooding or ponding long enough to turn its upper part anaerobic.
The Army Corps of Engineers and the Environmental Protection Agency use that committee's definition in administering Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (1972).

definition.text: A wetland that accumulates peat, a deposit of dead plant material, often sphagnum moss.

facts.text: Bogs, one of the four main wetland types, typically have peat over 30 centimetres thick, take most water and nutrients from precipitation, and are nutrient-poor and strongly acidic.
Unlike fens they get little mineral-rich ground or surface water, and rain lacks the calcium, magnesium and carbonate that would buffer the acidity of atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Plant growth is slow, but decay is slower still in oxygen-poor saturated bog soils, so peat accumulates, sometimes many metres deep.
Bogs form mostly in cooler northern climates in poorly draining lake basins, and are widespread in boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Valley bogs fill gently sloping valleys or hollows with peat and, because they rely on ground or surface water, occur only on acidic substrates.
Quaking bogs are floating mats of sphagnum anchored by sedges, about half a metre thick, over water or very wet peat, which move underfoot.
Low oxygen combined with high acidity and tannic acids preserves organic material in bogs, including bog bodies buried thousands of years ago.
Undisturbed bogs are carbon sinks; once peat is extracted the wetland is hard to restore because peat accumulates slowly.

definition.text: An acidic, mineral-poor bog fed only by precipitation, whose peat has risen into a dome above the groundwater.

facts.text: Many begin as fens under groundwater influence; lack of oxygen and high acidity stop decay, peat builds up, and the bog rises above the groundwater to become rain-fed.
Others grow straight on mineral ground poor in salts without passing through a fen stage.
Growth needs precipitation that exceeds losses to discharge and evaporation and falls evenly through the year; European raised bogs have grown for about 11,000 years.
Rootless peat mosses grow upward while lower layers turn to peat, adding about a millimetre a year.
A living upper acrotelm, where new organic matter forms, lies over the water-saturated, less active catotelm; light white peat overlies well-humified black peat.
The dome is typically a few metres high, often fringed by fen where groundwater seeps in at the edges or along streams.
Subtypes include coastal, plateau, upland, string and polygonal bogs.
Raised bogs are badly threatened by peat cutting and mineral pollution from farms and industry; the last great raised bog regions are in western Siberia and Canada.

definition.text: Peatland that forms where high rainfall and low evapotranspiration let peat cover broad stretches of rolling ground, not just wet hollows.

facts.text: It needs rain on more than about 235 days a year, which keeps the ground surface waterlogged much of the time.
It is commonest on acidic substrates but can form on neutral or even alkaline ones where acidic rainwater outweighs groundwater.
It is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere, well studied in Ireland and Scotland and covering vast areas of North American tundra, but less developed in the Southern Hemisphere.
In parts of Europe its spread is traced to forest clearance by prehistoric peoples.

definition.text: A semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or saturated, permanently or seasonally, so that oxygen-poor processes take place in its soils.

facts.text: Wetlands sit between open water and dry land, and their plants' roots are adapted to oxygen-poor waterlogged soil; one short definition is a community of hydric soil and hydrophytes.
There are four main kinds: marsh, with herbaceous plants; swamp, with woody plants; and bog and fen, which are peatlands or mires.
Wetlands are also grouped by water source: tides, mixed tide and river water in estuaries, overflowing rivers on floodplains, and rain or meltwater for bogs.
The US Cowardin system has five types: marine, estuarine, riverine, lacustrine and palustrine.
US regulations define wetlands as land inundated or saturated often and long enough to support plants adapted to saturated soil, and hydric soil is part of that legal definition.
About 60% of the world's wetlands are made of peat.
Wetlands exist on every continent except Antarctica; the largest include the Amazon basin, the West Siberian Plain, the Pantanal and the Sundarbans.
The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found wetlands more threatened than any other ecosystem; since 1971 the Ramsar Convention has protected wetlands of international importance.

title: Fen

definition.text: A peat-accumulating wetland fed by mineral-rich ground or surface water.

facts.text: Fens are one of the main wetland types with marshes, swamps and bogs; fens and bogs, both peat-forming, are together called mires.
Their ground or surface water input gives them higher mineral concentrations and a more basic pH than bogs.
Fen soils are constantly inundated because the water table is at or near the surface, and oxygen diffuses in so slowly that they are anaerobic.
Groundwater chemistry, set by the rocks the water passes through, controls a fen's pH; fens tend to lie over calcium-rich rocks such as limestone.
As peat builds up, groundwater input can be cut off, so a fen turns ombrotrophic and more acidic and may become a bog.
Locally fens lie where land meets water, such as the headwaters of streams and rivers; an estimated 1.1 million square kilometres exist worldwide.
Draining a fen lowers the water table, aerating and drying the peat so that it decomposes aerobically or even burns.
Cutting off groundwater inflow, for example by nearby quarrying, makes a fen more rain-fed, acidifying it and changing its water chemistry.

contested_note: Sources call it controversial whether fens are net sinks or net sources of greenhouse gases, because microbes in their anaerobic soils produce methane (S:0aadd030ffdd, S:16fa21fd6cf2).

definition.text: The arrangement of bogs and fens along a gradient from poor to rich, with bogs at the poor end, extremely rich fens at the rich end and poor fens between.

facts.text: 'Rich' and 'poor' refer to species richness, which depends strongly on pH and on calcium and bicarbonate concentrations.
Rich fens are strongly minerotrophic, fed by water dominated by calcium and bicarbonate, and are neutral to slightly acidic, about pH 7 to 5.
Groundwater passing limestone dissolves some calcium carbonate, and the bicarbonate produced buffers the fen's pH and keeps it relatively stable.
In extreme rich fens, often pH 7 or above, calcium carbonate precipitates as marl when plants or the atmosphere draw dissolved carbon dioxide down.
At high calcium concentrations calcium binds phosphate, so rich fens are not always very productive.
Poor fens, about pH 5.5 to 4, have thicker peat that cuts plants off from the mineral soil below and weakens groundwater buffering, making them more ombrotrophic.
Poor fens also form where the supplying groundwater flows through poorly soluble, weakly buffering sediments such as sand.
Sphagnum mosses acidify fens, and their spread can turn a rich fen into a poor fen.

definition.text: The cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements in wetland soils, which sit at the interface of oxygenated and oxygen-free environments.

facts.text: Most wetlands have a thin oxygenated top layer over a reduced layer, and microbes adapted to each oxidize and reduce nutrients as they cycle between them.
The reduced layer hosts denitrification, manganese, iron and sulfate reduction, and methanogenesis.
Organic carbon in a wetland is respired to CO2, buried as peat or decomposed to methane; peat builds up where plant production exceeds decomposition.
Methanogenic archaea in anaerobic peat make methane from CO2 and hydrogen; sedge and brown-moss fens emit more methane than sphagnum bogs.
Ammonium from anaerobic decay diffuses up and is nitrified in the oxidized layer; the nitrate diffuses down and is denitrified to nitrogen gas and some nitrous oxide.
Nitrogen and phosphorus limit wetland fertility, and almost all phosphorus arrives in sediment or plant litter from other ecosystems.
Iron can bind phosphate to toxic levels, but peat supplies organic anions that iron binds to instead.
Because wetlands are hotspots and sinks for nutrient transformations, they can be constructed to treat nutrient-rich waters.

definition.text: The benefits wetlands give society, such as carbon storage, water purification, flood control and wildlife habitat.

facts.text: Wetland plants take up and store nutrients from runoff and remove nitrate, and slow the water so that sediment, with any heavy metals it carries, settles out.
Floodplains act as natural reservoirs, spreading floodwater wide to cut its depth and speed, while headwater wetlands slow runoff and snowmelt.
Peat-forming wetlands sequester large quantities of carbon that would otherwise reach the atmosphere as CO2.
Replacing these services would take huge spending on water treatment plants, dams and levees, and many cannot be replaced at all.

title: Marsh

definition.text: A wetland dominated by herbaceous rather than woody plants.

facts.text: More loosely, the word means any low-lying, seasonally waterlogged ground; in Europe and farming literature it also covers meadows needing drainage and embanked polderland.
Marshes often edge lakes and streams, forming a transition between aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems.
Vegetation sets them apart: swamps are dominated by trees, and mires have built up deposits of acidic peat.
Marsh pH tends to be neutral to alkaline, unlike the acid conditions under which bog peat accumulates.
Marsh plants must survive in wet mud low in oxygen, so many have aerenchyma that carry air down to their roots.
The three main types, salt marshes, freshwater tidal marshes and freshwater marshes, differ mainly in location and salinity.
Salt marshes lie on sheltered, tide-washed coasts such as lagoons and estuaries, and flourish where sediment builds up faster than the land sinks.
Marshes hold 0.1% of global sequestered terrestrial carbon, and most natural marshland is threatened by sea level rise and the erosion it brings.

notes: Marsh says marshes hold 0.1% of global sequestered terrestrial carbon (S:72bd5431073d); Freshwater marsh says freshwater marshes hold as much as a third of the world's organic carbon (S:7fbab8b358b0). The measures differ but the gap is large; the second claim is not used.

definition.text: A freshwater marsh that is regularly flooded but often dry in summer.

facts.text: Wet meadows occupy shallow lake basins, low-lying depressions, the ground between shallow marshes and uplands, and the edges of large lakes and rivers.
They often have very high plant diversity and dense stores of buried seeds.
As a wet meadow matures, decomposing vegetation thickens the soil into hummocks above the water where shrubs and small trees take root, a route toward shrub swamp.

definition.text: A seasonal marsh in a shallow depression that holds shallow water in winter and spring and may be completely dry by summer and fall.

facts.text: Vernal pools form where an impermeable or very slowly permeable layer, such as a duripan, claypan or lava flow, underlies a small depression and perches the water table.
In California they often fill the hollows between Mima mounds, on old, strongly developed soils with a claypan or silcrete duripan in the subsoil.
They drain only internally, being cut off from perennial inflow, yet hold ponded water at least briefly in most years.
Being free of fish, they are spring breeding sites for many amphibians.

definition.text: A marsh in one of the many shallow depressions left by glaciers across northern North America.

facts.text: Glaciers once covered these landscapes and left shallow depressions in great numbers, which fill with water in spring.
Some hold water only seasonally, while others stay wet all year.
Small wetlands such as prairie potholes can contribute significantly to recharging regional groundwater.
They are important breeding habitat for many species of waterfowl.

title: Mima mounds

definition.text: Low, flattened, circular to oval natural mounds of loose, unstratified, often gravelly sediment forming an overthickened A horizon.

facts.text: They range from 3 m to more than 50 m across and from 30 cm to over 2 m high, at densities of several to more than 50 mounds per hectare.
Proposed origins include burrowing by pocket gophers, wind-blown sediment caught around plants, earthquake shaking, and shrink–swell clays as in gilgai.
Mounds tend to occur on poorly draining soils, and tracers showed gophers pushing soil up toward mound centres, though they may only maintain existing mounds.
In California they sit on stable landforms over 100,000 years old whose claypan or duripan perches water into vernal pools between the mounds.

contested_note: Sources give competing explanations for how Mima mounds form, and it has not been shown that all such mounds share one cause.
notes: Crawled page in no chapter's dossier; drafted here as a soil-landscape microrelief (how-soils-form cites it under Dynamic denudation).

definition.text: A forested wetland, with saturated soils or standing water dominated by water-tolerant woody plants.

facts.text: Swamps are transition zones shaped by both land and water, and their water may be fresh, brackish or seawater.
Freshwater swamps form along large rivers or lakes and depend on rain and seasonal flooding for natural swings in water level; saltwater swamps line tropical and subtropical coasts.
They are characterized by saturated soils and slow-moving water fed by precipitation, groundwater, tides and freshwater floods.
Hydrology is a key control on a swamp's biogeochemical environment, including oxygen, nutrients, pH and toxicity.
As water moves through a swamp, nutrients, sediment and pollutants are filtered out, and excess chemicals end up buried in bottom sediment.
The two main types are true swamps, or swamp forests, and transitional shrub swamps.
Some swamps are peatlands, such as peat swamp forests; like fens, swamps have higher pH and nutrient availability than bogs.
The largest swamp is the Amazon River floodplain, and other very large ones lie along the Mississippi and Congo.

definition.text: The draining, filling and conversion of wetlands for agriculture, building and other uses.

facts.text: Wetlands have decreased by as much as 50% since 1900 and by 90% in some parts of the world; Europe has likely lost nearly half of its wetlands.
Wetlands are often diked and drained for farming, and the settlements built on them then face subsidence and rising flood risk, as in the Mississippi delta around New Orleans.
More than 50% of Europe's original mire area, once over 300,000 km², has been lost to drainage for agriculture and forestry and to peat harvesting.
Restoration often begins by plugging drainage ditches, removing levees, or returning channelized rivers to their natural course so that they flood again.

definition.text: A wetland whose soils consist of organic matter from decaying plants, forming layers of peat.

facts.text: Peatlands arise where waterlogging and the resulting lack of oxygen leave plant litter only partly decomposed.
Ecologists apply the term to any terrain with peat at least 30 cm deep, even if it has been completely drained.
Formation is controlled mainly by precipitation and temperature, but relief matters too, since waterlogging comes more easily on flat ground and in basins.
Mires occur where organic matter stays waterlogged, so their distribution depends on topography, climate, parent material, biota and time.
Peat formation typically starts by paludification of forest on mineral soil, terrestrialisation of lakes, or primary peat formation on bare, once-glaciated soils.
Accumulating peat raises the ground above the original topography; depths above 10 m are common in temperate regions and above 25 m in the tropics.
Peat's high cation-exchange capacity swaps cations such as Ca²⁺ for H⁺, so water passing through loses nutrients and pH, and mires are acidic unless groundwater inflow is high.
Peatlands cover about 3% of the globe's surface; around a quarter of their area is used for agriculture and forestry, which means ditches to lower the water table.

definition.text: A peatland that is still actively forming peat.

facts.text: Drained and converted peatlands may keep a peat layer but are not mires, because new peat no longer forms.
The two types are bogs, raised above their surroundings and fed only by precipitation, and fens, on slopes, flats or in depressions and fed by groundwater or the surrounding mineral soil.
All mires begin as fens and may become bogs once the peat rises above the surrounding land.
Some swamps are also peatlands, but marshes, whose plants root in mineral soil, generally are not.

title: Peatland carbon storage

definition.text: The accumulation of carbon in peatland soils, which makes peatlands the largest natural carbon store on land.

facts.text: Though covering just 3% of Earth's land, peatlands hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon, over half the amount in the atmosphere.
Plants take in CO2 by photosynthesis at the surface, while living plants respire some back and litter and peat lose more through heterotrophic respiration.
Natural mires are a small CO2 sink but generally net emitters of methane and nitrous oxide; over millennia they have had a net cooling effect on the atmosphere.
The water table is the main control: a high one submerges peat and slows respiration, while a falling one, as in drought, speeds aerobic decomposition and CO2 release.
Methanogens make methane in anoxic peat below the water table and methanotrophs oxidize some of it above, so water level sets the size of both zones.
Warmer soils raise seasonal methane flux; one Alaskan study found methane varying by as much as 300% between seasons.
Draining a mire lets oxygen into the peat column, upsetting the balance of accumulation and decay and turning a net carbon sink into a net emitter.
Northern peatlands built up mostly in the Holocene after the Pleistocene glaciers retreated, and their total carbon stock is estimated at 1055 Gt.

conflicts.text: Northern peatlands store an estimated 415 Gt of carbon.
conflicts.note: Peatland gives 1055 Gt C for total northern peat carbon stocks (S:34ca5dac5e2b).

conflicts.text: Globally, peat stores up to 550 Gt of carbon.
conflicts.note: Peatland gives 500 to 700 billion tonnes (S:aab06bdb534a) and, in its lead, over 600 Gt (S:76a49ee066cf).

notes: The 1055 Gt northern stock (S:34ca5dac5e2b) exceeds the 500–700 Gt global figure on the same page; the verification pass should check which estimate each cites.

definition.text: A peat-forming ecosystem of northern, mostly Arctic and boreal, climates, roughly synonymous with bog or peatland.

facts.text: It is a standard term in Canada and Alaska, from the Cree maskēk, 'low-lying marsh'.
Muskeg is organic material in various stages of decay, from fairly intact sphagnum to sedge peat to highly decomposed humus, with wood making up five to fifteen percent.
It forms where permafrost, clay or bedrock blocks drainage so that rain and snowmelt collect, and it needs abundant rain and cool summers.
In water or saturated soil, low oxygen and cool temperatures hold back bacteria and fungi, so plant debris decays slowly and builds up as peat.
Its sphagnum holds fifteen to thirty times its own weight in water, so muskeg can form even on sloping ground; depending on the topography it can exceed 30 metres deep.
It is wet, acidic and relatively infertile, with the water table near the surface, so large trees cannot grow.
Muskeg hampers transport: heavy equipment has sunk into it as frozen muskeg thawed in spring, and building may require removing it and filling with gravel.
Uncleared muskeg's high water content makes it buckle when it freezes; log corduroy roads, or cheaper winter ice roads, are used to cross it.

definition.text: A region of highly fertile, loess-covered lowland in North Germany, a 'fertile plain'.

facts.text: Börden are large, flat, nearly treeless areas of fertile loess soil, particularly important for arable farming.
They stretch from the North German geest to the edge of the Central Uplands, on loess laid down mainly by east winds, up to 10 metres thick, that evens out the relief.
The loess overlies boulder clay in some places and Mesozoic and Tertiary sedimentary rock in others; under a (sub-)oceanic climate it has been largely decalcified and turned to loam.
Their black earth soils are among the best in Germany, and the northern edge of the loess marks a soil, vegetation and settlement boundary.

definition.text: The vertical variations in the micro- and macro-relief of a soil surface, together with their statistical distribution.

facts.text: Four classes are recognized by vertical scale: grain-to-aggregate microrelief of 0.053–2.0 mm, clods of 2–100 mm, tillage-oriented roughness of 100–300 mm, and macro-scale topographic curvature.
The first two classes make up microroughness, which rainfall changes over single events and tillage over seasons.
Microroughness is usually measured as Random Roughness, the standard deviation of surface heights about the mean after correcting for slope and removing tillage effects.
Rainsplash tends to smooth a rough surface, but on smooth surfaces with initial microroughness of about 0–5 mm rainfall can raise it considerably.

definition.text: The washing of loose soil or sediment down through fissures in the rock beneath, one of the two processes that form subsidence sinkholes.

facts.text: It occurs where loose soil, loess or other non-cohesive material lies over limestone with fissures and joints; rain and surface water carry it into caves below, leaving a surface depression.
Most sinkholes form this way rather than by collapse of an underlying cave or void.
Suffosion sinkholes are usually linked to karst, though they can form in chalk, gypsum and basalt.

Suffosion collapses soil structure, losing both mass and volume as coarse grains lose contact; suffusion instead removes fines from between coarse grains that stay in contact, with no change in volume.

definition.text: A form of mass wasting in which a coherent mass of loosely consolidated material or rock moves a short distance down a slope.

facts.text: The mass slides on a concave-upward or planar surface; translational slumps move on planes such as joints or bedding, especially where a permeable layer overlies an impermeable one.
In a rotational slump the block slides on a concave-upward surface and rotates backward, so its original surface becomes less steep.
A cliff-like scarp forms where the mass breaks away; back-tilted block tops can hold ponds or swampy ground, and hummocky ridges form near the toe.
Causes include earthquakes, thorough wetting, freezing and thawing, undercutting and loading; removal of the slope base by stream or wave erosion or road building is a common trigger.
Rain lubricates the material and adds to its weight, so slumping often follows heavy rainfall and storms.
Added water and lost cohesion at the toe can turn slumping material into an earthflow.
Speeds range from metres per second to metres per year; sudden slumps may stabilize within hours, but most take months or years.
On steep hillsides slumps often run along fracture zones in materials like clay, and much stream-bank erosion happens as weakened banks fail in large slumps.

title: Polder

definition.text: A low-lying tract of land enclosed by dikes that forms an artificial hydrological unit.

facts.text: Polders are land reclaimed from a lake or seabed, floodplains cut off from sea or river by a dike, or marshes diked and then drained.
Water enters through groundwater seepage and pressure, rainfall, or rivers and canals, so the excess must be pumped out or let out through sluices at low tide.
Drained marsh ground subsides, and peat polders sink as their peat decomposes on exposure to air, so all polders eventually lie below the surrounding water some or all of the time.
Polders lie mostly in river deltas, former fenlands and coastal areas, and are at constant risk of flooding.
Dike materials carry their own risks: sand can collapse when saturated, and dry peat, lighter than water, may fail to hold water in very dry seasons.
Embanked and drained tidal marshes go by the Dutch name polder, Marschland in northern Germany, and marine clay districts in the Netherlands and Belgium.
The Dutch have turned marsh and fenland into some 3,000 polders, and as much as 20% of the Netherlands has at some time been reclaimed from the sea.
Earthworms moving into recent polders have been seen to improve soil structure.

conflicts.text: By 1961 about half of the Netherlands' land, 18,000 km², had been reclaimed from the sea.
conflicts.note: The same page's lead says as much as 20% of the land area was reclaimed from the sea (S:09be4b8a616b).

notes: Peat (S:cd384479fc77) dates the first Dutch polder to probably 1533; Polder puts the first polders in the 11th century and the oldest surviving one (Achtermeer) in 1533. Probably compatible (oldest extant vs first built).

title: Ombrotrophic

definition.text: Describing soils or vegetation that receive all their water and nutrients from precipitation rather than from streams or springs.

facts.text: The word means 'cloud-fed', from the Greek ómbros, rain, and trophē, food.
Ombrotrophic sites are hydrologically isolated from the surrounding landscape, and because rain is acidic and very low in nutrients, they host organisms tolerant of acid, nutrient-poor conditions.
Their hydrology follows climate: precipitation supplies water and nutrients, and temperature sets how fast water evaporates.
Ombrotrophic conditions can arise even over nutrient-rich rock: in high-rainfall areas limestone boulders may be capped by acidic bog vegetation.
Ombrotrophic bogs rely solely on precipitation and atmospheric dust for nutrients, though their slowly decaying peat releases some, such as easily mobilized zinc, copper and manganese.
Base-poor environments are typical where the rock beneath the soil is sandstone or granite, or where water comes directly from rainfall.
Mercury and lead stay immobile in ombrotrophic peat, so these bogs serve as records of past atmospheric mercury deposition.
High nitrogen deposition in Europe has shifted peatland plants toward more vascular biomass and less Sphagnum, the moss that holds moisture and nutrients and aids carbon sequestration.

notes: CONTESTED flag on S:8c32f77cd77b (whether nitrogen deposition keeps raising carbon accumulation in Canadian bogs) is open uncertainty, not a debate between sources.

definition.text: A non-forested marsh with shallow fresh water that is continuously or frequently flooded.

facts.text: Freshwater marshes usually lie near river mouths, along lakes, or in poorly drained low ground such as abandoned oxbow lakes, and get most of their water from surface water.
Their soils are hydric: saturated in the growing season, high in organic matter because decomposition is slow, and often black or brown.
Microbes use up the oxygen, and anaerobic processes then accumulate or deplete reduced iron and other minerals, giving the soils a distinctive morphology.
Types include river, lacustrine, tidal freshwater and palustrine depressional marshes, the last in isolated depressions or on hill slopes and often fed by springs or seepage.

definition.text: Describing environments that get their nutrients mainly from groundwater flowing through mineral-rich soil or rock, or from surface water flowing over land.

facts.text: Such water has picked up dissolved chemicals that raise nutrient levels and reduce acidity.
Where the dissolved chemicals include bases such as calcium or magnesium ions, the water is called base-rich and is neutral or alkaline.
Fens and rich fens are often minerotrophic, while poor fens and bogs are often ombrotrophic; marshes and swamps may also be partly fed by groundwater.
Ions brought in by a wetland's hydrology set its pH, conductivity and nutrient levels, which differ between discharge- and recharge-dominated settings and change with seasonal groundwater levels.
Geology, soil type and surface form also shape a wetland's character alongside its hydrological setting.
Steady groundwater supplies of water and nutrients support diverse plants and let peat accumulate, provided the water does not flow too fast.
'Minerogenous' and 'geogenous' are often used as synonyms, though they refer mainly to hydrology, and minerotrophic to nutrient dynamics.

title: Shrub swamp

definition.text: A freshwater wetland dominated by shrubs, too wet to become swamp forest but too dry or shallow to become marsh.

facts.text: Often seen as transitional between wet meadows or fens and conifer or hardwood swamps, shrub swamps follow floods, cutting, fire or windstorms in forested swamps, or develop from drained meadows and fens.
Their water comes from runoff, streams and rivers and moves in and out through the year, so they are drier than wet meadows or forested swamps, and less water-tolerant plants grow on hummocks.
They typically occur on organic soils such as muck and shallow peat.
Some classifications require at least 50% shrub cover and less than 20% tree cover.

notes: S:219c656afb7a carries a WHICH? tag: the classification setting the 50%/20% cover limits is unnamed.

definition.text: The most common way boreal peatlands form, as peat builds up on previously drier, vegetated mineral soils and turns forest, grassland or bare land into peatland.

facts.text: Organic soil starts and thickens over inorganic soil with no fully aquatic phase; peat can also start by terrestrialisation of lakes.
It requires a positive, wet hydrological balance in the growing season, the balance being precipitation minus evapotranspiration and runoff.
External factors such as climate, geomorphology, geology and soils usually control that balance, but local peat accumulation alone can also drive paludification.
Tree removal, natural or human-caused forest fires, more precipitation and podzolization can shift the water balance toward paludification.
Flat, low-slope topography matters, as in the world's two largest peatlands, the West Siberian Plain and the Hudson/James Bay Lowlands.
Heavy clay mineral soil acts as an impermeable substrate that lets water collect, and surface water from melting permafrost can increase paludification.
In boreal forests it lowers soil temperature, aeration, nutrient availability and decomposition rates, and can lead to permafrost forming.

title: String bog

definition.text: A bog of slightly raised ridges and islands carrying woody plants, alternating with flat, wet sedge mats.

facts.text: String bogs lie on gently sloping ground, with ridges 2–3 m wide and under 1 m high set at right angles to the water flow, and wet pools between them.
Their water and peat, which is over 1 m thick, are very low in nutrients because the water drains from other ombrotrophic wetlands.
They are a patterned form of blanket bog in periglacial climates, where the active layer stays frozen for long periods and thaws in spring.
They are also called aapa mires, from the Finnish, or Strangmoor, from the German.

title: Hummock

definition.text: A small knoll or mound above the surrounding ground, usually under 15 metres high and found in groups or fields.

facts.text: In raised bogs such as string bogs, hummocks are low ridges of drier peat moss alternating with shallow wet depressions called flarks.
Swamp hummocks usually start as moss-covered fallen trunks or branches rising above the swamp floor, with low hollows between them.
Cryogenic earth hummocks form in permafrost and seasonally frozen ground, usually in moist, fine-grained soils of low relief; differential frost heave is the most widely accepted explanation.
Digging into them often reveals a disturbed profile streaked with organic matter, a form of cryoturbation reaching about as deep as the hummock is high.

title: Palustrine wetland

definition.text: Any inland, non-tidal wetland whose ocean-derived salts stay below 0.5 parts per thousand.

facts.text: The category takes in inland marshes and swamps as well as bogs, fens, pocosins, tundra and floodplains.
It is one of five systems in the Cowardin classification of the US Fish and Wildlife Service; the others are marine, estuarine, riverine and lacustrine wetlands.
Its vegetation classes are aquatic bed, emergent, scrub-shrub and forested, with woody plants 20 feet tall dividing the last two.
Palustrine depressional marshes sit in hydrologically isolated depressions or on hill slopes, and include vernal pools, playas and prairie potholes.

title: Land loss

definition.text: The conversion of coastal land to open water by natural processes and human activities.

facts.text: It is broader than coastal erosion, also covering land lost around estuaries, bays and lakes and by subsidence of coastal wetlands.
Its main causes are coastal erosion, inadequate sediment supply, subsidence and sea level rise.
Large deltas, including the Danube, Ganges, Mississippi, Nile and Yellow, have all suffered significant land loss.

title: Salt marsh

definition.text: A tidal wetland in the upper intertidal zone, regularly flooded by seawater or brackish water and dominated by salt-tolerant plants.

facts.text: Its plants trap and bind sediment; marshes form as tidal flats build up by sediment accretion until vegetation can colonize them.
High sedimentation and abundant organic matter keep marsh sediments reliably anoxic, an ideal home for sulfate-reducing bacteria.
Bacteria and fungi drive nutrient cycling by remineralizing organic matter; bacteria degrade up to 88% of the lignocellulose.
Nitrifiers such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrosospira and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are common in marsh sediments.

notes: Assigned to this chapter by the concept graph; most of the page is coastal geomorphology. Facts kept to its soil-forming sediments and their nutrient-cycling microbes; soils-in-the-landscape (Marsh seed) may be a better home.

title: Flark

definition.text: A depression or hollow within a bog, typically one of a series of parallel hollows separated by ridges called strings.

facts.text: Early theories blamed frost heaving, but flarks have since been found where frost heaving does not occur.
They are now thought to form when thickening peat slides downslope under its own weight and tears away below obstructions in the underlying terrain.
Another theory ties them to patches of the bog that decay faster.

notes: Assigned here by the concept graph through its frost-heaving link; it fits Soils in the landscape (Bog, Peatland) better.

definition.text: The flow, storage and chemistry of surface and ground water in a wetland, the main factor that produces wetlands.

facts.text: How long flooding or groundwater saturation lasts decides whether a wetland carries aquatic, marsh or swamp vegetation.
Water enters as precipitation, surface water and groundwater and leaves by evapotranspiration, surface flow, tides and subsurface outflow; the balance sets the hydroperiod.
Most wetlands are minerotrophic, but ombrotrophic bogs fed only by precipitation have water low in minerals; fens range from acidic to alkaline and calcium-rich.
Wetlands can recharge groundwater when the surrounding water table is low and discharge it when the table is high.

definition.text: An artificial wetland built to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater.

facts.text: It uses plants, soil and organisms for secondary treatment, removing suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen and phosphorus.
Like natural wetlands it acts as a biofilter for pathogens and heavy metals, and subsurface-flow wetlands remove more pathogens than surface ones.
Constructed wetlands are also built to reclaim mined land or to make up for natural wetlands lost to development.
The East Kolkata Wetlands, a natural system covering 125 square kilometres, treat Kolkata's sewage, and its nutrients feed fish farms and crops.

definition.text: The release of methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from wetland soils, which makes wetlands the largest natural source of atmospheric methane.

facts.text: Wetlands supply about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average about 161 Tg a year.
Microbes in warm wet soil use oxygen faster than it diffuses in, creating the anaerobic conditions methanogens need; warmth and organic-rich soil boost methane output.
Draining peat exposes carbon stored for thousands of years to air, where it decomposes to CO2; peatlands cover 3% of land, but their degradation gives 7% of all CO2 emissions.
Some wetlands emit nitrous oxide, with 300 times the warming potential of CO2, though wetlands can also act as greenhouse gas sinks.

title: Ramsar Convention

definition.text: An international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, also called the Convention on Wetlands.

facts.text: It was signed at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971, came into force on 21 December 1975 and has 172 parties.
Its definition is broad: marsh, fen, peatland or water, natural or artificial, fresh, brackish or salt, including sea no deeper than six metres at low tide.
In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres; the United Kingdom has the most sites, 175.
2 February is World Wetlands Day, first celebrated in 1997, but national follow-through on the treaty is often half-hearted.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

definition.text: The strip of land where a river or stream meets the land around it.

facts.text: Its vegetation of water-loving plants matters for soil conservation, biodiversity and the health of aquatic ecosystems.
It acts as a natural biofilter, shielding water from excess sediment, polluted surface runoff and erosion.
Meanders, plants and roots slow the water, reducing soil erosion and flood damage, and trapped sediment replenishes soils and builds banks.
It lowers nitrate from manure and fertilizer in runoff, largely by denitrification, and wetland riparian zones remove nitrate especially fast.
Where ground beside a stream holds standing water or saturated soil for a season, it is normally called a wetland because of its hydric soils.
Streamside plants shade the water; thinning them brings higher and more variable water temperatures.
Zones damaged by building, farming or forestry are usually restored through erosion control and revegetation.

definition.text: Land beside a river, from the channel banks to the valley sides, that floods when discharge is high.

facts.text: Its soils are flood-laid clays, silts, sands and gravels, and regular floods bring nutrients that make them fertile; the Nile and Mississippi basins farm floodplains heavily.
Most floodplains grow by deposition of point bars on the insides of meanders, called lateral accretion, while the outer bank erodes, and by overbank flow.
Overbank flow, every one to two years on undisturbed rivers, leaves a thin veneer of sediment, coarsest and thickest by the channel; this is vertical accretion.
Most sand drops on natural levees beside the channel, while silt and clay settle farther out as floodplain mud.
Floodplains hold far more sediment than the river load and are major sediment stores; an abandoned floodplain may survive as fluvial terraces.
Every 10–1000 years a river may abandon its channel belt and build a new one elsewhere, a process called avulsion.
Draining floodplains or narrowing them with levees weakens their flood control, so floods become more severe.

definition.text: The soils of floodplains, which vary with small changes in elevation and swing between aerated and flooded states.

facts.text: They stay aerated between floods, but saturated soil can run out of oxygen if floodwater stands long enough; higher ground farther from the river holds more oxygen.
Soil microbes alternate between aerobic and anaerobic activity, which affects fine-root growth.
Floodplains buffer phosphorus strongly, keeping it from reaching the river, especially when they stay connected to the stream.
Wet–dry cycles shift redox state, pH and minerals, so formerly flooded soils that dry out hold phosphorus more tightly.

definition.text: A peat mound with a permanently frozen core of peat and mineral soil, typical of mires in the zone of discontinuous permafrost.

facts.text: Palsas can be up to 150 m (490 ft) across and 12 m (39 ft) high, with steep slopes rising above the mire.
Wet or frozen peat lets cold in during winter, while dry surface peat insulates the core in summer, so palsas survive where mean annual temperature is just below freezing.
They start where thin snow lets frost go deeper; an ice lens grows by drawing in water and lifts the surface by frost heave, a positive feedback.
Warming thaws the frozen peat, thickening the active layer and wetting the mire, which raises methane emissions.

title: Peat swamp forest

definition.text: A tropical moist forest whose waterlogged soil keeps dead leaves and wood from fully decaying, building a thick layer of acidic peat.

facts.text: It holds far more carbon as soil organic matter than forest on mineral soil, among the largest near-surface stores of land organic carbon.
Peat starts on deltas, floodplains or oxbow lakes fed by rivers, then domes up to 4 m on coasts or 18 m inland, becoming rain-fed and strongly acidic.
About 62% of tropical peatland lies in the Indomalayan realm, 80% of it in Indonesia, and 36% lies in Africa's central Congo Basin.
Indonesia's Mega Rice Project from 1996 drained over 1 million hectares of Borneo peat forest; peat fires, drainage and clearing release the stored carbon as CO2.

definition.text: A cone-shaped spread of sediment that fans out from a concentrated source, such as a narrow canyon opening onto a plain.

facts.text: Fans form where flow leaves a confined channel and spreads out, losing the capacity to carry its sediment.
They range from less than 1 square kilometre to almost 20,000 square kilometres, with slopes of 1.5 to 25 degrees, steepest near the apex.
Their sediments are coarse and poorly sorted, coarsest at the apex and finer towards the edge.
Blocked channels periodically shift (nodal avulsion), so only part of a fan is active and bypassed areas undergo soil formation or erosion.
Inactive lobes may develop desert varnish or a soil profile from windblown dust over 1,000 to 10,000 years.
Fans are fed either by debris flows or by stream flow; hyperconcentrated flows carry 20% to 45% sediment, between sheetfloods and debris flows.
Their coarse beds form aquifers that are the main groundwater reservoirs in many regions, and cities such as Los Angeles and Salt Lake City sit on them.
Neighbouring fans can merge into a continuous apron called a bajada, and a channel shift on the Kosi River fan caused catastrophic flooding in 2008.

definition.text: The compass direction that a land surface faces, also called exposure.

facts.text: Together with slope grade, aspect describes the surface gradient, and its effects on a slope's physical and living features are called the slope effect.
In the Northern Hemisphere north-facing slopes are often shaded, while south-facing slopes receive more solar radiation per unit area.
Aspect shapes local microclimate: south-facing slopes in the Northern Hemisphere are generally warmer and drier, with more evapotranspiration.
Steep equator-facing slopes have soil organic matter levels like level ground at lower elevation, while pole-facing slopes resemble level soils higher up.
Outside the tropics, slopes facing the early-afternoon sun usually have the lowest soil moisture and organic matter in a locale.
Windward soils tend to be shallower with more developed subsoils, while leeward soils receive more windblown particles.

definition.text: The scientific study of the origin and evolution of landforms created by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near Earth's surface.

facts.text: Surface processes include water, wind, ice, fire and life acting on the land, along with the chemical reactions that form soils.
Landforms evolve from the balance of additive processes (uplift and deposition) and subtractive ones (subsidence and erosion).
Its processes fall into producing regolith by weathering and erosion, transporting it, and depositing it.
Soil geomorphologists read soil profiles and chemistry to learn a landscape's history and how climate, biota and rock interact.
Soil, regolith and rock move downslope by creep, slides, flows, topples and falls, with burrowing and tree throw setting some hillslope rates.
Weathering is usually studied by soil scientists but is essential to geomorphology because it supplies the material that can be moved.
Its practical uses include landslide prediction and mitigation, river control, stream restoration and coastal protection.

definition.text: The total soil component of the non-living matrix of an ecotope.

facts.text: It is not one kind of soil, or even the dominant one, but all the soils of every variety present at a location.

title: Hydrosere

definition.text: The plant succession by which an area of open fresh water fills in and becomes land, ultimately woodland.

facts.text: Early changes are driven by sand and clay washed in from the catchment; later, plant remains add to the infill, and the whole succession takes centuries or millennia.
Dead plankton decay into humus that mixes with inwashed silt and clay to form soil, making the pond shallower.
Reed rhizomes knit the mud and their decay-resistant litter builds reed peat; sedge peat eventually rises above the water so the soil is no longer waterlogged.
Overall the succession builds up the substrate, adds humus and minerals, and builds and aerates soil.

contested_note: Sources say it is still debated whether dry woodland is always the final climax or whether a bog community can be a stable climax.

definition.text: The change over time in the erosion rates, erosion styles and shape of the slopes of hills and mountains.

facts.text: Three models dominated most of the 20th century, slope decline, slope replacement and parallel slope retreat, and slope form was central to geomorphology until the 1950s.
In William Morris Davis's slope decline, slope angle falls gradually as stream incision slows and slopes fill with fine regolith from weathering.
Walther Penck's slope replacement, tied to slowing denudation, starts with flattening of the lowest slope that spreads upward and backward: flattening always occurs from the bottom up.
Parallel retreat needs constant rock strength and steady removal of basal debris such as talus; that is rare, except where a hard cap rock such as basalt overlies softer rock.
Lester King championed parallel scarp retreat and pediplains as globally dominant, and saw slope decline as a special case in very weak rocks.
King linked convex-concave slopes without a free face to grass carpets that slowed surface wash and so gave relatively more soil creep.
Under unequal activity, a term coined by Colin Crick, slopes in an area do not all develop at once; with little river erosion, slopes may be effectively stagnant.
Modern work holds that slope evolution is far more complex than the classical models of decline, replacement and retreat imply.

definition.text: Numerical models of hillslope erosion that describe the sediment flux on a slope at a given time rather than how its form changes.

facts.text: Taking Fourier's heat equation as a template, W.E.H. Culling wrote sediment flux as q = −K∇z, where K is a rate constant (L2/T) and ∇z the slope gradient.
The linear law lets flux be estimated from slope angle, which holds for low-angle slopes but not for steep ones.
A nonlinear version adds a critical gradient Sc: as the gradient nears Sc, erosion rates become extremely high, which may represent landslides on steep terrain.
Steep slope angles change very little even when erosion rates rise greatly, so erosion rates cannot be read from steep topography.

definition.text: Convex, soil-covered hills long held to reflect a steady-state balance between soil production and soil erosion.

facts.text: The idea goes back to the work of Grove Karl Gilbert (1909) and William Morris Davis (1892).
Soil depth on such hills can vary considerably because bedrock weathers into soil stochastically, so soil formation rates may differ greatly across a landscape in equilibrium.
Numerical models suggest broad low-angle convex hilltops in periglacial settings take no less than millions of years to form.
Convex hills are often associated with tors, and many tors suggest the original landscape was steeper than today's.
